title: old Fraser digs the trench across the southern road
summary: In the last week of an t-Samhain, with frost already hard on the ground, old Fraser digs the trench across the southern cart-road into Muileann àrsaidh, deep enough to stop a laden cart and narrow enough for a man to cross on foot. He tells Ruth Calder plainly what the digging is for.

title: The spoil wall left unfinished at its northern end
summary: old Fraser leaves the last length of the pit-yard wall unbuilt, calling it exhaustion; the town understands it as his own caution against finishing a wall built all the way round, which would look too near a boast.

title: Ruth Calder begins the letter to the council
summary: At her father's table above the pit-head, on a windy night in an t-Samhain, Ruth Calder writes the salutation of a letter to the council of the kingdom and no more, the first of several attempts she will tear across before the letter is finished.

title: Ruth Calder tears up a draft written as a grievance
summary: A second attempt, three paragraphs on the wrong done the towns by the Leòid ruling, is torn across unfinished; Ruth Calder judges it would read at the Library as one more northern complaint among many and be filed the same way.

title: Sarah Dunmore counsels an offer and not a complaint
summary: In her kitchen at Muileann àrsaidh, Sarah Dunmore tells Ruth Calder that four years of letters have argued a right and never once made an offer, and that the towns' one thing worth offering is their coal, on their own terms.

title: Ruth Calder drafts the offer of the Crown's fifth in coal
summary: On the last evening of an t-Samhain, Ruth Calder writes the third draft of her letter: the five towns will pay the Crown's fifth in coal on every load raised, from that day until the seams are spent, if the Board will carry it and press no further claim.

title: The four pit captains allow Ruth Calder to sign for them
summary: Weeks before the letter is finished, Ruth Calder asks the pit captains of Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg whether she may set their names beneath her own if the letter says nothing they would not themselves say; none refuses her.

title: The five towns keep Christmas at Àth leathan's chapel
summary: On the morning of the twenty-fifth of an Dùbhlachd the chapel at Àth leathan is filled with its own people and others come down from Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais, the western hills keeping the feast together, both faiths of the island under one roof as the coast has long done.

title: Ruth Calder copies the letter fair and signs it
summary: In a borrowed room at Àth leathan on Christmas afternoon, Ruth Calder copies her letter fair in a plain ledger hand, dates it, and signs it with her own name and the names of the other four pit captains beneath it.

title: Tom Varley walks the letter to the post at the western Seann Skell
summary: Tom Varley walks the five miles from Àth leathan to the western Seann Skell on Christmas evening and gives Ruth Calder's letter over the post office counter before it closes for the feast.

title: Ruth Calder's letter posted at the western Seann Skell
summary: The post clerk at the western Seann Skell enters Ruth Calder's letter in his book among the season's other correspondence and sends it north three days after with the ordinary carrier.

title: The letter laid on the table at Leabharlann Muileann chaol
summary: In the second week of am Faoilleach the letter reaches Leabharlann Muileann chaol, is entered in the day-book in the keeper's own clerk's hand, and is laid on the table of the council's business beside what else waits there.

title: A copy of the letter kept in the Moot's minute
summary: A copy of Ruth Calder's letter is carried to Caol mhòr and set down in the Moot's own minute, under a heading giving only what it was and when it came, though the Moot itself is no party to it.
